Decision Trees

Every model you have trained so far hid behind a wall of math. This chapter cracks the wall open: a model that literally writes its own if/then rulebook by asking useful questions of the data, splitting the answers, measuring how mixed each group is, and recursing until every leaf tells you both the prediction and how confident it is. You will build a tree by hand, race Gini against entropy, watch a tree memorize noise when its depth is uncorked, see the same tree predict numbers instead of labels, rotate the data and gasp at how the questions change, and finally confront the model's most painful flaw: change one training example and a completely different tree comes out.

✍️ "Orthogonal decision boundaries are sensitive to data rotation — always consider PCA preprocessing."

Your Journey Through Chapter 6

Fourteen topics, roughly 4–5 focused hours — and the order is the lesson: every new technique exists because the previous one hit a wall. You will start by training and visualizing your first decision tree, then learn how to follow a prediction path through it, then ask how confident a leaf really is, then crack open CART (the training algorithm that grew the tree in the first place), then race Gini against entropy, then tame the tree with regularization, then turn the same idea into a regression model, then rotate the data and gasp at the new questions, and finally confront high variance — the disease that makes small data changes produce wildly different trees. Progress is tracked in the bar above as you scroll.

🧭 Orientation — who this is for

You need zero probability theory or calculus — this chapter teaches the tiny slice of impurity and entropy it uses, from intuition first. If you can read a flowchart and follow "a tree follows a path," you are qualified. Every term arrives in this order: plain meaning → story → technical meaning → example, and each topic stands on the ones before it, exactly like a real tree-building session.

You do not need to run any code to follow along — every code-shaped idea (DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree, the CART objective) is explained in plain language first, with the equations built symbol by symbol. If you are reading Hands-On Machine Learning alongside, treat each topic here as a warm-up and a second opinion for the matching part of Chapter 6. Chapters 2–4 are referenced only where a tree idea needs them (training/test split, classification basics, cost functions) — never re-taught.

◆ The running story

The Project You Will Live Inside

Chapter 6 is not a list of tree algorithms — it is one continuous engineering campaign to build a model the operations team can read aloud and trust. Before Topic 1, meet the people whose tree you are about to grow. Everything on this page happens inside their world.

🎬 The Setup — Tuesday, 7:14 a.m., the loading dock

June's new rule: "If you can't read it, don't ship it"

Three months after the energy-forecasting win of Chapter 4, Meridian Mail Systems runs into a wall that no regression model can climb. The hub is upgrading its 6 a.m. priority truck to a 4 a.m. departure, which means every parcel that previously made the morning truck now needs to be triaged the night before — into three buckets: priority (next-day air, expensive but fast), standard (afternoon ground, the workhorse), and economy (next-day bulk, the cheapest). The team has 24 historical parcels with three measured features (weight in grams, distance to destination in kilometers, declared value in dollars) and the bucket each one was eventually routed to. The procurement director wants a model that decides the bucket automatically — and June has a new rule.

"If I can't read the model's reasoning out loud to a dock worker," June says, tapping the table, "I can't put my signature on it. The dock team has 90 seconds per parcel and zero patience for black boxes. I don't care how accurate your neural network is — if it can't tell me which rule fired, it's a paperweight." Tomás, who has been quiet for most of the meeting, grins. "Decision trees. A model that literally writes its own if/then rulebook by asking useful questions of the data. We can print the tree on a single laminated card and ship it to the dock."

Ravi opens his laptop. "I've used scikit-learn's DecisionTreeClassifier before — it's three lines of code. But I've never actually... read what comes out." Tomás nods slowly. "That's exactly what this chapter fixes. By the end of today, you'll be able to draw a decision tree by hand, follow a parcel from root to leaf, calculate Gini impurity in your head, tell me why entropy usually picks the same split (but not always), explain why an unrestricted tree memorizes noise, turn the same tree into a regression model that predicts delivery hours, rotate the data and watch the questions change, and diagnose why one flipped example produces a completely different tree. You will own the whole machine."

💡 This chapter is the story of that Tuesday — and the two weeks of triage system work that follow it: starting with a single question that splits the 24 parcels in half, discovering impurity as the yardstick that grades a split, racing Gini against entropy, letting the tree grow too deep on purpose to watch it memorize, taming it with hyperparameters, watching it predict numbers instead of labels, rotating the data and gasping at the new questions, and finally confronting the model's most painful flaw — high variance — that sets up the ensemble methods of Chapter 7.

💼 Real parcel→ ❓ Ask: weight? distance?→ 🔀 Split the data→ 📏 Measure impurity→ ♻️ Recurse→ 🛑 Stop→ 🍃 Leaf→ 🔮 Class & probability→ 📋 Read-aloud rule Ask → Split → Measure → Repeat → Stop → Predict → Diagnose. The entire chapter in one chain.

👩‍💻 Ravi — you

Three months older than the engineer who started Chapter 4, comfortable with linear models and gradient descent — but new to a model that grows its own structure. He can call DecisionTreeClassifier — now he has to read what comes out, break it, fix it, and defend it to a dock team with 90-second triage windows.

💼 June — the operations boss

Owns the dock, the trucks, and the routing card. Asks the questions that hurt: "Why did the tree pick weight as the first question?", "Why is one parcel mis-routed?", "Why does the tree change when I correct one label?" Her signature is the audit trail of this chapter.

🛠️ Tomás — the veteran

Has debugged tree models since before scikit-learn's plot_tree existed. Keeps a laminated decision tree in his notebook for the lab room's parcel triage. Every lab in this chapter is something he once broke in production.

The dataset this story runs on

All numbers in this chapter come from a small, original, fictional dataset written for teaching: 24 historical parcels, each with three measured features (weight in grams, distance in kilometers, declared value in dollars) and a route label (priority, standard, or economy). The 24 parcels are plausible, self-contained, and sized so you can verify every impurity calculation by hand — they are not the book's iris or moons dataset, and every character and company here is fiction. The same 24-parcel dataset feeds the regression arc (Topic 12), where the target becomes "delivery hours" instead of "route bucket."

◆ The engine of this page

The Five Laws of Learning

Most pages teach decision trees by listing formulas for impurity. This page makes you live them: you will predict the first split before the algorithm reveals it, break the tree on purpose by uncorking its depth, compress each rule into a single sentence, feel what an unstable tree costs a real hub, and decide what only a human can certify. Learn the loop once — then recognize its colors in all fourteen topics below.

The learning loop you will run 14 times today

What should you notice? Prediction comes before explanation everywhere on this page. Struggling for 30 seconds before an answer is shown is not wasted time — it is the mechanism. The struggle builds the "hooks" the answer locks onto.

⚡ Law 1 — Prediction Before Explanation

Guess before you know

Before every topic, a blue box asks you to commit to a written guess — "which question should the tree ask first?", "what's the Gini of a 50/50 node?", "which depth will overfit?". You will be wrong surprisingly often; that's the point. A wrong prediction that gets corrected creates a memory far stronger than a passive read ever could.

🔴 Law 2 — Failure Modes Over Features

Study the cracks, not just the paint

Every topic gets a red section asking four questions: Why was this technique invented? What does it quietly assume? How does it fail silently? What rescues it? Decision-tree failures — trees that memorize noise, axis-aligned splits that miss diagonal boundaries, single-example flips that produce different trees — are the most expensive failures in applied ML, and this law trains you to spot them unprompted.

🟢 Law 3 — Compression Beats Coverage

If you can't shrink it, you don't own it

After each topic, a green box asks you to explain it to a 12-year-old in one paragraph — then compares your attempt against an expert compression, a one-diagram version, and a one-sentence version. Fourteen tree concepts you can't compress are fourteen concepts you'll scramble by Friday.

🟡 Law 4 — Emotion Creates Judgment

Feel the cost of being wrong

Each topic includes Engineer Stakes: a realistic scenario where a tree mistake costs Meridian real money — an unpruned tree that memorizes 24 parcels and mis-routes a high-value shipment, a probability leaf of 1.0 taken as a guarantee, a high-variance tree that routes differently on Monday than on Tuesday. Emotionally encoded knowledge is what you'll retrieve under interview pressure.

🟣 Law 5 — AI Accelerates, Humans Judge

Use the machines; keep the verdict

Every topic ends with a purple section splitting the work into two piles: what AI tools can reasonably do (draft tree-building boilerplate, compute Gini tables, render plot_tree outputs, sweep hyperparameters, generate exercises) and what you must own (is the first split domain-sensible? is the tree too deep? do the leaf probabilities mean anything? is the tree stable? what does the model physically say?). You get a ready-to-use AI prompt and a "verify this yourself" checklist. Modern decision-tree work is human + AI; this law trains the human half. AI can compute the tree; only you can certify the tree means something.

Journey rail ① Visualize→ ② Predict→ ③ Rules→ ④ Probability→ ⑤ CART→ ⑥ Diagnose

01 Topic 1 of 14

Training and Visualizing a Decision Tree

Before any algorithm, before any impurity formula, before any regularization knob — there is a model made of nothing but questions. This topic is the atom every later concept is built from: a root, a split, a branch, a leaf, and a prediction you can read aloud to a dock worker.

🎬 The Story — A laminated card for the dock

Ravi trains his first tree and tries to read it

Tomás pushes a printout across the table: a 24-row spreadsheet of historical parcels, each with three numbers (weight, distance, value) and a label — priority, standard, or economy. "Three lines of code," he says. "Import DecisionTreeClassifier, fit it on the 24 rows, and out comes a tree. The question is whether you can read it."

Ravi types the three lines. The model returns in milliseconds — far faster than any model in Chapter 4 ever did — and out comes a tree with one root question, two child questions, and four leaves. He traces it with his finger: "distance ≤ 17 km? If yes, weight ≤ 320 g? If yes, priority. If no, standard. If distance > 17, distance ≤ 50? If yes, standard. If no, economy." He blinks. "That's it? The whole model is four if/then rules?"

"That's the whole model," Tomás says. "Every decision tree, no matter how complex, is a flowchart you can print on a single page. The complexity lives in how many questions the tree asks before reaching a leaf — but each individual question is dead simple: is feature X above or below a threshold? The tree picks the feature and the threshold for you, automatically, by trying every candidate and grading the resulting split." He taps the root of Ravi's tree. "Today we start with the anatomy. Tomorrow we crack open the algorithm that chose this root question and not some other one."

💡 The whole of Chapter 6 lives inside that laminated card: a tree is just nested if/then rules, the tree picks its own questions by minimizing impurity (Topic 5–9), unrestricted growth is what causes overfitting (Topic 11), the same recursion works for regression (Topic 12), and axis-aligned splits + the recursive nature are exactly what makes the tree sensitive to rotation and to single-example changes (Topics 13–14). The card is the chapter, compressed.

📊 Dataset (24 parcels)→ 🌳 Root node→ ❓ First question→ 🔀 Branch→ 🌿 Internal node→ 🍃 Leaf → prediction Root → Question → Branch → Internal node → Leaf. The whole anatomy of a tree.

⚡ Law 1 — Predict Before Explanation

Before You Learn: What Do You Think?

"The model will be allowed to ask one of three first questions: weight ≤ ?, distance ≤ ?, or value ≤ ?. Before you see the answer, write down which feature you think the tree will pick first, and why."

The Correction

The honest answer is "I don't know yet" — because the tree's choice depends on which question most reduces impurity on the 24 training examples, and we haven't defined impurity yet (Topic 5). But here is what most people miss: the tree does not pick the question that "looks most important to a human." It picks the question that, numerically, produces the cleanest children. On this dataset, it happens to pick distance ≤ 17 as the root — but it could have picked weight or value, depending on exactly how the 24 examples cluster. The lesson: "which feature is most important?" is a question about the data, not about your intuition.

A common second guess is "weight, because heavy parcels obviously cost more to ship." That's a reasonable domain prior, and it would be true if the tree were built by a domain expert — but CART builds trees by exhaustive search over candidate thresholds, and the winner is whichever (feature, threshold) pair minimizes weighted child impurity. Sometimes that aligns with intuition, sometimes not. The tree is a description of what the data rewards, not what the world rewards.

What should surprise you?

The surprise is that you can build a useful model without choosing your own questions. The whole point of CART (Topic 5) is that the algorithm tries every feature at every candidate threshold and picks the best one — the engineer's job is not to design the tree but to constrain it (Topic 11). That shift in perspective — from "I write the rules" to "I bound the rules the machine writes" — is the entire mental model of modern tree-based ML.

What changed in your mental model?

🧠 The idea, explained three ways

🧢 Everyday analogy

Think of the world's simplest guessing game: "I'm thinking of an animal — ask yes/no questions to figure out which one." Twenty Questions, but with the questions pre-decided for you by someone who studied the data. Each question splits the remaining candidates roughly in half, and after a few splits only one candidate remains. A decision tree is exactly that: a 20-questions game where the questions were chosen by an algorithm that tried every possible question and picked the one that most cleanly separated the remaining examples.

🎬 In our story

June's dock worker has 90 seconds per parcel. A 4-leaf tree with 2 questions fits on a laminated card the worker can scan in 5 seconds. Ravi's job is not to design the questions — CART did that. His job is to verify each question is domain-sensible (does "distance ≤ 17 km" make operational sense for the priority-truck cutoff?), to verify the leaves are clean (a 9-of-9 priority leaf is a confident rule; a 5-of-9 priority leaf is a coin flip wearing a label), and to feed the tree new data when it arrives.

🔬 Technical view

A decision tree is a recursive partitioning of feature space into axis-aligned rectangular regions. Each internal node tests one feature against a threshold (x_j ≤ t); the left branch holds examples that satisfy the test, the right branch the rest. Recursion continues until a stopping condition fires (pure leaf, depth limit, min-samples limit) at which point the node becomes a leaf holding a prediction: the majority class (classification) or the mean target (regression). The whole tree is a piecewise-constant function over the feature space.

Why this matters in a real ML system

Because the structure IS the model. A linear regression's parameters are deliverables; a decision tree's structure is the deliverable — which features it split on, in what order, at what thresholds. Interpretability, audit, regulatory approval, and the dock team's trust all read the structure directly. When a stakeholder asks "why did the model predict X?", a tree lets you point at a path: "because distance ≤ 17 and weight ≤ 320, so it landed in the priority leaf." That directness is the tree's superpower — and, as Topics 13–14 will show, also its most fragile property.

A 24-parcel decision tree, fully grown to depth 2

What should you notice? The root split on distance ≤ 17 km sent 9 of the 24 parcels left, of which 8 are priority — a clean child. The right child got 15 parcels, of which 7 are economy — also reasonably clean. The tree then recursed on both children. Two of the four leaves are perfectly pure (priority 8/9 and economy 7/7 in this representation), and two are imperfect but majority-class. The tree is not "right" — it is a description of where the data lives. If you added a 25th parcel that broke the pattern, the tree might restructure itself.

The point: the tree doesn't ask the question that looks important — it asks the question whose children are cleanest.

🛠️ What "training a tree" means to an engineer

Strip away the mystique and training a decision tree is: pick a structure (recursive binary splits), pick an impurity criterion (Gini or entropy — Topics 7–8), find the (feature, threshold) that minimizes weighted child impurity at each node, recurse until a stopping rule fires. That recursion is the entire training algorithm (CART, Topic 5). Unlike gradient descent from Chapter 4, there is no learning rate, no convergence, no cost curve to monitor. The tree grows deterministically — the same data produces the same tree, byte-identical. (Until Topic 14 breaks that promise.)

🛠️ Reading the structure like a practitioner

The tree's structure is the deliverable: feature split order, threshold values, leaf compositions. When June asks "why is this parcel priority?", the answer is a path through the tree — and that path is what you defend. A practitioner checks four things on a freshly trained tree: (1) Is the root split domain-sensible? (2) Are the leaves clean (low impurity, sufficient samples)? (3) Is the depth reasonable (a depth-20 tree on 24 rows is overfit — Topic 11)? (4) Are there leaves with too few samples to trust (a 1-of-1 leaf is a memorization, not a rule)?

🔴 Law 2 — Failure Modes Over Features

How This Breaks: when the tree fits the data instead of the problem

🧬 Why was this needed?

Because "design a flowchart by hand" doesn't scale. A domain expert can hand-write rules for a 2-feature problem with 50 examples; nobody can hand-write rules for a 30-feature problem with 100,000 rows. CART exists to automate the rule-discovery process: try every candidate question, grade every resulting split, recurse. It converts taste into arithmetic.

🤫 What it quietly assumes

That the data is separable by axis-aligned splits (Topic 13 will break this), that the impurity criterion is the right grading scheme (Topic 7), that the leaves contain enough samples to be statistically meaningful (Topic 11), and that the training data is representative of the deployment data (everywhere). All four are assumptions, not facts.

💀 How it fails silently

It fits beautifully and lies anyway. An unrestricted tree on 24 training parcels can produce a 24-leaf tree where every leaf is one parcel — 100% training accuracy, perfect memorization, zero generalization. The tree looks flawless; it has learned the training set's noise, not its pattern. Worse, training accuracy always rises as you allow deeper trees — so the metric that feels like quality is, in fact, the opposite of quality past the optimal depth.

🔧 What happens next?

Four rescues follow. First, we crack open CART (Topic 5) to see how the splits are actually chosen. Second, we compare Gini and entropy (Topics 7–9) — sometimes they save us from a bad split, sometimes they pick the same one. Third, we deploy regularization (Topic 11) to stop the tree from growing too deep. And fourth, in Topic 14, we admit that even a well-regularized tree is unstable — and Chapter 7 arrives with the ensemble cure.

Failure file — the 1-of-1 leaf that routed a $400 parcel as economy

A fulfillment team shipped a decision tree with 47 leaves on 200 training examples. The tree achieved 100% training accuracy; one leaf contained a single example — a heavy, far, high-value parcel routed as economy. When a similar $400 parcel arrived in production, the tree routed it through that 1-of-1 leaf and shipped it economy, costing $260 in surcharge. The post-mortem found the leaf was a memorization of one noisy training example, not a rule; the team had never audited leaf sizes. Lesson: a tree's training accuracy tells you nothing about its leaves' quality. Always inspect leaf sizes, not just overall accuracy — and never trust a 1-of-N leaf where N is small.

🧩 Important Terminology

Decision Tree

Simple: a flowchart the model writes for itself by asking useful questions of the data.

Technical: a recursive partitioning of feature space into axis-aligned rectangular regions, each ending in a leaf that holds a prediction.

see glossary →

Root node

Simple: the first question the tree asks — every prediction starts here.

Technical: the topmost internal node; the split that has the largest impurity reduction across all training examples.

see glossary →

Internal node

Simple: a non-leaf node that asks another question.

Technical: a node that tests one feature against a threshold and has exactly two child branches (in CART's binary form).

see glossary →

Leaf node

Simple: where the questions stop — the tree's final answer for any example that lands here.

Technical: a terminal node holding a prediction (majority class for classification, mean target for regression) and a class-probability distribution over its training members.

see glossary →

Split & threshold

Simple: the question a node asks: "is feature X ≤ this number?"

Technical: a binary test x_j ≤ t; the threshold t is chosen from the unique observed values of x_j in the node's training subset.

see glossary →

Branch

Simple: the "yes" or "no" answer that sends an example down one of two paths.

Technical: the left branch (test satisfied) or right branch (test failed) — each child node receives the corresponding training subset.

see glossary →

Tree depth

Simple: how many questions deep the longest path through the tree goes.

Technical: the length (in edges) of the longest root-to-leaf path; the maximum number of splits any single prediction traverses.

see glossary →

Prediction (at a leaf)

Simple: the leaf's majority class — what the tree says the example is.

Technical: for classification, argmax over the leaf's class-proportion vector; for regression, the leaf's mean target.

see glossary →

🟢 Law 3 — Compression Beats Coverage

Compress It

"Explain what a decision tree is in one paragraph, as if you were explaining it to a 12-year-old."

Expert compression

Imagine a game of 20 questions where the questions are already picked for you, based on what worked on thousands of examples. The model holds up a new example at the top of a flowchart and asks the first question — "is distance less than 17 km?" If yes, it walks down one branch to the next question; if no, down the other. After a few questions it lands at a final box called a leaf, and the leaf says "this is a priority parcel" — that's the prediction. The clever bit is that the questions themselves were chosen by trying every possible question and keeping the ones that most cleanly separated the answers. The whole model is just a laminated if/then card you can read aloud.

One-diagram version
📊 data→🌳 root question→🔀 branch→🌿 more questions→🍃 leaf → answer
One-sentence version

A decision tree is a flowchart that the model writes itself by asking useful yes/no questions of the data, recursively, until each leaf is confident enough to make a prediction.

Memory hook

🌳 "A sequence of questions, each one halving the possibilities, until the answer is clear."

🟡 Law 4 — Emotion Creates Judgment

Engineer Stakes

Scenario — the 1-of-1 leaf that misrouted a high-value parcel

Meridian's procurement director signs off on Ravi's first decision tree — 24 parcels, depth-5, 100% training accuracy. Two weeks later a $400 declared-value parcel arrives, weight 1280 g, distance 71 km. The tree routes it through a leaf containing a single training example (one heavy, far parcel labeled "economy"), predicts economy, and the parcel ships next-day bulk. The customer demands a refund for the late delivery: $260 surcharge, plus a reputation ding. The post-mortem asks the question every decision-tree engineer must learn to ask: did we audit the leaves?

What went wrong? A 100% training-accuracy tree is not a sign of quality — it's a sign of memorization. The 1-of-1 leaf was noise, not a rule. Was the tree or the leaf-sizes the problem? The leaf sizes — the tree's structure was fine; what was missing was a min_samples_leaf constraint. What evidence should have been collected? A leaf-size histogram: count how many leaves contain fewer than 5 training examples. What should be changed first? Re-train with min_samples_leaf=5 and re-audit. What should NOT be changed blindly? Swapping to a different model family would have re-hidden the same disease behind more complexity.

🏗️ Build in Public Challenge

Take any small dataset you personally care about (10 rows × 3 features is plenty — study hours vs. sleep vs. previous score → pass/fail). Call DecisionTreeClassifier on it, render the tree with plot_tree, and read the first split out loud. Ask: does this question make sense? If yes, ship it. If no, dig into why the algorithm picked it. You will have personally read more tree structure than most people who say "I trained a model."

🟣 Law 5 — AI Accelerates, Humans Judge

AI vs Human Judgment — Building the first tree

🤖 AI Should Handle

  • Writing the DecisionTreeClassifier boilerplate with clean comments and reproducibility settings
  • Generating synthetic small datasets to practice tree-building on
  • Rendering the trained tree as an SVG or text diagram via plot_tree
  • Computing impurity tables across candidate thresholds so you can see the comparison
  • Drafting the leaf-size histogram and depth summary statistics

🧑‍⚖️ Humans Must Own

  • Is the root split domain-sensible? Does "distance ≤ 17" make operational sense for the priority-truck cutoff?
  • Are the leaf sizes safe? Are there leaves with 1 or 2 samples that are memorizing noise?
  • Is the depth reasonable? A depth-10 tree on 24 rows is memorization; a depth-2 tree might be the right shape.
  • Do the predicted classes make sense for the leaves' compositions? Is a 6-of-9 leaf "confident enough"?
  • The call: does this tree generalize, or does it merely describe the 24 training rows?
What would you ask AI?"Here is a 24-row parcel dataset with three features (weight, distance, value) and a route label (priority/standard/economy). Write a small, well-commented scikit-learn script that trains a DecisionTreeClassifier, prints the tree's depth, leaf count, and the size of every leaf, then renders the tree with plot_tree. Then list three domain-specific reasons the root split might NOT match operational intuition."
What must you verify yourself? Check the root split against operational knowledge — does ~17 km match the priority-truck catchment radius? Sanity-check leaf sizes — a leaf with 1 sample is a memorization, not a rule. And look at the tree diagram with your own eyes: AI-generated tree reports reliably print depth and leaf counts, but they won't spontaneously tell you "this 1-of-1 leaf is a noise memorization that will mis-route a real parcel." AI can train the tree; only you can certify the leaves mean something.

🎤 Interview Question

✅ Quick Check — Training and Visualizing a Decision Tree
🧒 Beginner lens

A decision tree is a model that asks yes/no questions about your data, one after another, until it knows enough to make a prediction. The first question is called the root. Each question splits the data into two groups — those that answer yes go down one branch, those that answer no go down the other. Eventually the questions stop and you reach a leaf, which is the model's answer. The clever bit is that the tree picks its own questions by trying every possible one and keeping whichever most cleanly separates the answers. You don't design the tree — you bound it.

🔬 Technical lens

Structurally, a CART tree is a binary tree where each internal node carries a predicate x_j ≤ t and two child pointers. The leaves hold a class-proportion vector (classification) or a scalar mean (regression). Training recursively partitions feature space into axis-aligned rectangles; at each node, the algorithm enumerates every (feature, threshold) pair where the threshold is a mid-point between consecutive sorted observed values, computes weighted child impurity for each, and selects the argmin. The structure is deterministic given the data — no stochasticity, no learning rate, no convergence. Scikit-learn exposes this via DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='gini', max_depth=None, min_samples_split=2, min_samples_leaf=1); the defaults are intentionally permissive, which is exactly why you must learn to constrain them (Topic 11).

🎤 Interview lens

• "A decision tree: a recursive partitioning of feature space into axis-aligned regions, each leaf holding a majority-class prediction. CART grows it by picking, at each node, the (feature, threshold) that minimizes weighted child impurity."
• Follow-up to expect: "Why axis-aligned? Why not diagonal splits?" — because each internal node tests one feature against one threshold; diagonal boundaries require multiple sequential splits (Topic 13).
• Reflex to display: distinguish the structure (the splits, the order, the thresholds) from the leaves (the predictions, the class proportions) — both are deliverables, but they answer different stakeholder questions.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A decision tree is a recursive flowchart the model writes itself by asking yes/no questions of the data — each question is a feature-threshold test, each answer routes down a branch.
  • The four anatomical parts are: root (first question), internal nodes (subsequent questions), branches (yes/no paths), leaves (predictions).
  • The tree picks its own questions by trying every candidate split and choosing whichever most reduces impurity in the children — the engineer's job is not to write rules but to bound them (Topic 11).
  • A tree's structure (which features it split on, in what order, at what thresholds) is itself a deliverable — interpretability, audit, and stakeholder trust read the structure directly.
  • Training accuracy is not quality: an unrestricted tree can hit 100% by memorizing every training example, which is the opposite of generalization.
  • Always inspect leaf sizes — a 1-of-1 leaf is a memorization, not a rule, and it will mis-route the next real example that lands in it.
Journey rail ① Visualize→ ② Predict→ ③ Rules→ ④ Probability→ ⑤ CART→ ⑥ Diagnose

02 Topic 2 of 14

Making Predictions — Following a Path

Topic 1 ended with a trained tree on the table. The next question is operational: when a new parcel arrives, how does the tree decide? The answer is a single walk from root to leaf — but the way you read that walk determines whether the model is a black box or a transparent rule.

🎬 The Story — A new parcel walks the tree

The 4:14 a.m. parcel that didn't fit any training row

It's 4:14 a.m. on the second Tuesday of the triage system's deployment. A new parcel arrives on the dock: weight 240 g, distance 14 km, declared value $42. Ravi types the three numbers into the tree. The root question is "distance ≤ 17 km?" — 14 ≤ 17, so yes, go left. The next question is "weight ≤ 320 g?" — 240 ≤ 320, so yes, go left again. The leaf says priority, with class composition 8/9 priority. Done. The whole prediction took two feature comparisons and was over in 90 seconds — exactly what June's dock team asked for.

"But wait," Ravi says, staring at the path. "None of the 24 training parcels had this exact combination of features. How can the tree predict priority for an example it never saw?" Tomás nods slowly. "Because the tree doesn't match examples — it partitions feature space. Every parcel that satisfies distance ≤ 17 km and weight ≤ 320 g lands in that leaf, and the leaf's majority class is priority. The tree has drawn a rectangular region in (distance, weight) space and labeled it priority. Your new parcel happens to land inside that region — so it inherits the region's label."

💡 This is the single most important mental shift in Chapter 6: a decision tree does not retrieve similar training examples — it partitions the input space and labels each region. Every parcel that lands in the same region gets the same answer. The tree is a piecewise-constant function over feature space, and prediction is just "which region does this input fall into?"

📦 New parcel→ 🌳 Root question→ 🔀 Branch left/right→ 🌿 Next question→ 🍃 Leaf → label Root → Question → Branch → … → Leaf. The traversal is the prediction.

⚡ Law 1 — Predict Before Explanation

Before You Learn: What Do You Think?

"A parcel arrives with weight 740 g, distance 28 km, value $115. Following the tree from Topic 1, which leaf does it land in — and what does the tree predict?"

The Correction

Trace it: root asks distance ≤ 17 km? — 28 ≤ 17 is false, so go right. Right child asks distance ≤ 50 km? — 28 ≤ 50 is true, so go left. Left child of the right node is the leaf labeled standard (composition 8/15 standard). The parcel is predicted as standard, regardless of its weight or value — because those features are not on this particular root-to-leaf path. The tree's structure decided which features mattered for this parcel; weight and value simply weren't asked.

This is the key insight: a tree does not ask every feature of every example. It asks only the features that lie on the traversal path. A feature split high in the tree is asked of every example; a feature split deep in the tree is asked of only the examples that reached that depth. This is what makes trees so much more interpretable than linear models with 30 features — a path explains exactly which features mattered for this specific prediction, in order, with the thresholds that decided it.

What should surprise you?

The surprise is that two parcels with very different weights can land in the same leaf if their distance happens to be the same on the traversal path. The tree "ignores" features that aren't on the path — not because they're unimportant in general, but because they're uninformative for this prediction. That's profoundly different from a linear model, where every feature contributes a coefficient-times-value to every prediction. The tree's locality of feature importance is what makes its explanations so crisp.

What changed in your mental model?

🧠 The idea, explained three ways

🧢 Everyday analogy

Imagine a maze where every junction has a sign: "if you weigh less than 50 kg, go left; otherwise go right." You walk in at the entrance, follow the signs, and end up at exactly one exit. The exit doesn't care what path you took through the maze — only that you arrived here. A decision tree is exactly such a maze, where the signs were chosen to make each exit as homogeneous as possible.

🎬 In our story

Ravi's dock worker doesn't need to understand the tree — only to read the signs. "Is distance less than 17 km? Yes? Go to question 2. Is weight less than 320 g? Yes? Priority bucket." The whole interaction is 90 seconds and zero math. This is the operational superpower of decision trees: prediction is a deterministic walk, and any literate non-technical user can perform it from a printed card.

🔬 Technical view

Prediction is a descent from root to leaf. At each internal node, evaluate the predicate x_j ≤ t; if true, follow the left child pointer, else the right. Recurse until a leaf is reached; the leaf returns its stored prediction (majority class for classification, mean target for regression). Cost is O(depth) — typically logarithmic in the number of leaves for a balanced tree, independent of training set size. This is the asymmetric bargain of decision trees: training is expensive (Topic 10), but prediction is cheap.

Tracing a 4:14 a.m. parcel through the tree

What should you notice? The parcel only saw two of the four leaves — and only the features on its path. The right child's distance ≤ 50 km? question and the leaves under it are invisible to this prediction. This is the locality of feature importance: the tree asks each example only the questions on its traversal path. A different parcel going through the right branch would see a completely different subset of the tree's structure.

🧪 Lab 2 — Follow the Path

Type in a parcel's three features (weight, distance, value) and the lab will trace its path through the Topic 1 tree. The path is highlighted in blue, and you can read out the sequence of questions the tree asked. Try several parcels — especially ones that visit the right subtree — to see how each prediction sees a different subset of the tree's structure.

240
14
42
Prediction: —  ·  leaf composition: —

Drag the sliders. Notice: the prediction only depends on the features along the traversal path — value ($) never gets asked on this particular tree. That's the locality of feature importance.

🛠️ What "predicting" means to an engineer

Prediction is a deterministic descent: start at the root, evaluate the predicate, follow the corresponding child pointer, repeat. The cost is O(tree depth) — typically a handful of comparisons, no matrix multiplies, no floating-point heavy work. That's why decision trees are extraordinarily cheap to deploy: a 6-deep tree makes 6 comparisons per prediction, regardless of whether the training set was 24 rows or 24 million. The training set size only affects the structure of the tree, not the cost of traversing it.

🛠️ Reading the path like a practitioner

A prediction path is itself a deliverable. When a stakeholder asks "why did the tree predict priority for this parcel?", the path is the answer: "because distance ≤ 17 km and weight ≤ 320 g, which puts it in a leaf where 8 of 9 training examples were priority." That path is the audit trail. A practitioner reading a tree checks two things on every prediction: (1) Does the path make domain sense? (2) Is the leaf's class composition confident enough to ship? If the leaf says "5-of-9 priority," the prediction is priority by majority vote but the model is hardly certain — that's a flag, not a verdict.

🔴 Law 2 — Failure Modes Over Features

How This Breaks: when the path is honest but the leaf lies

🧬 Why was this needed?

Because the previous model (a linear classifier from Chapter 4) couldn't tell the dock worker why a parcel was routed priority. It just produced a probability. The traversal-path story exists to make every prediction auditable in seconds.

🤫 What it quietly assumes

That the leaf composition is statistically meaningful — that 8-of-9 priority is genuinely a "priority" rule and not a small-sample fluke. The traversal is honest; the leaf might not be.

💀 How it fails silently

The path looks clean and confident — "distance ≤ 17, weight ≤ 320, leaf says priority" — but if the leaf composition is 5-of-9, the prediction is priority by a coin-flip majority. The path explains the routing; it does not validate the confidence. Reading the path without reading the leaf composition is reading the audit trail without the audit.

🔧 What happens next?

The rescues are: (1) Topic 4 introduces class probabilities as the leaf's composition, not just its majority — so confidence becomes readable; (2) Topic 11 constrains min_samples_leaf so no leaf has so few samples that composition is a fluke; (3) the Stability Lab (Topic 14) tests whether the path is stable under data perturbations.

Failure file — the 5-of-9 leaf that confidently routed a fragile parcel as standard

A dock team treated the tree's path as proof of confidence: "distance ≤ 50 km, weight ≤ 720 g, leaf says standard" was treated as a certain standard classification. The leaf composition was 5 standard / 4 economy — a coin flip wearing a label. A fragile $180 parcel was routed standard and damaged in transit; the customer sued for $1,800. The post-mortem: the team had never read leaf compositions, only the predicted labels. Lesson: the path tells you which rule fired; only the leaf's composition tells you how confident that rule is. Both must be audited.

🧩 Important Terminology

Prediction path

Simple: the chain of questions the tree asks of one example, from root to leaf.

Technical: the sequence of internal nodes traversed from root to a leaf for a given input; each node's predicate evaluated against the input's features.

see glossary →

Traversal

Simple: the act of walking an example through the tree, one question at a time.

Technical: the descent from root to leaf; cost is O(depth) — independent of training set size.

see glossary →

Leaf composition

Simple: the mix of training examples that ended up in this leaf — what the leaf "knows."

Technical: the class-count vector (or target-value list for regression) of the training subset that reached this leaf during training; the basis for both prediction and class-probability estimates.

see glossary →

Feature space partition

Simple: the way the tree slices up the space of all possible inputs into labeled regions.

Technical: the recursive axis-aligned rectangular partitioning of ℝⁿ induced by the tree's internal node predicates; each region corresponds to exactly one leaf.

see glossary →

🟢 Law 3 — Compression Beats Coverage

Compress It

"Explain how a decision tree makes a prediction, in one paragraph, as if you were explaining it to a 12-year-old."

Expert compression

Imagine a maze where every junction has a yes/no sign: "is your distance under 17 km? Yes? Go left." You walk in at the entrance, follow the signs, and end up at exactly one exit. The exit doesn't ask how you got there — it just looks at where you landed and announces: "priority." That's the whole prediction. The clever bit is that the maze was designed so each exit is mostly filled with one kind of example, so the exit's announcement is usually right. You don't need to be a math person to read the signs — you just walk.

One-diagram version
📦 input→🌳 root→🔀 branch→🌿 next node→🍃 leaf
One-sentence version

Prediction = a deterministic walk from root to leaf, where each internal node asks a feature-threshold question and routes the example down one of two branches.

Memory hook

🚶 "Walk the signs, read the exit."

🟡 Law 4 — Emotion Creates Judgment

Engineer Stakes

Scenario — the path that lied about its confidence

A new parcel lands in a 5-of-9 priority leaf. The path reads cleanly: "distance ≤ 17 km, weight ≤ 320 g, leaf = priority." The dock worker routes it priority. It's actually a borderline case — economy would have been a better choice given the customer's premium-economy contract preference. The cost of the wrong routing is $40 in additional handling. The path was honest; the leaf composition was the lie. June catches it in a Tuesday audit and asks the question every decision-tree engineer must learn: did you read the composition, or just the label?

What went wrong? The path was treated as proof; the leaf composition was ignored. Was the prediction wrong or the confidence wrong? The confidence — the leaf was a coin-flip wearing a label. What evidence should have been collected? The leaf's class-probability vector (Topic 4) — if priority share is 0.55, the dock team needs a fallback rule, not a confident routing. What should be changed first? Either retrain with deeper leaves (larger min_samples_leaf) or add a confidence threshold to the deployment logic: if no class share exceeds 0.7, escalate to a human sorter. What should NOT be changed blindly? Don't rip out the tree — its structure is fine; the deployment contract was missing.

🏗️ Build in Public Challenge

Take the tree you built in Topic 1's challenge. Pick any 5 unseen examples and trace each one's path by hand. Read out: which questions did the tree ask? Which features did it ignore? Which leaf did it land in? Post your traces — and the leaf compositions — for the public to verify. You will have performed more decision-tree audits than most people who say "I deployed a model."

🟣 Law 5 — AI Accelerates, Humans Judge

AI vs Human Judgment — Predicting with a tree

🤖 AI Should Handle

  • Writing the prediction boilerplate (tree.predict([parcel])) with input validation
  • Tracing paths automatically and producing a human-readable summary of the questions asked
  • Generating synthetic parcels to test edge cases (boundary values, unseen regions)
  • Drafting a per-leaf confidence report (composition vector, sample count)
  • Suggesting fallback rules when leaf composition is borderline

🧑‍⚖️ Humans Must Own

  • Is the leaf composition confident enough to ship the prediction? (5-of-9 ≠ 9-of-9)
  • Does the traversal path make domain sense — does the order of questions match operational reality?
  • Are there examples landing in low-sample leaves — and what's the deployment policy for them?
  • Is the tree being asked to extrapolate beyond its training region (a Topic 13 concern)?
  • The call: deploy as-is, deploy with confidence thresholding, or send to a human fallback?
What would you ask AI?"Here is my trained decision tree (24 parcels, depth 2). For this new parcel (weight=240, distance=14, value=42), trace the prediction path node by node, print the leaf composition, and tell me whether the leaf's confidence (majority share) exceeds 0.8. If not, suggest two operational fallback rules."
What must you verify yourself? Check the leaf composition with your own eyes — AI tools reliably trace paths but don't always distinguish a 9-of-9 leaf from a 5-of-9 leaf in their summary. Sanity-check whether the path is asking the features you'd expect: a tree that asks about value ($) when the operational reality is that distance matters is a tree to re-examine, even if its accuracy is high. AI can trace the path; only you can certify the leaf is confident enough to ship.

🎤 Interview Question

✅ Quick Check — Making Predictions
🧒 Beginner lens

When a new parcel arrives, the tree asks it the first question (the root). The answer takes it down one branch to the next question. The next answer takes it down another branch. After a few questions it lands at a leaf, and the leaf's label is the prediction. The clever bit: the tree only asks the questions on the path — so different parcels see different parts of the tree.

🔬 Technical lens

Prediction is a descent from root to leaf: at each internal node, evaluate x_j ≤ t against the input's feature vector and follow the corresponding child pointer. Recurse until a leaf is reached. Cost is O(depth) — independent of training set size, which is why trees deploy cheaply at scale. The path is itself a deliverable: it is the local explanation of why this prediction was made. Scikit-learn exposes the path via tree.decision_path(X) — useful for audit logs.

🎤 Interview lens

• "Prediction is a root-to-leaf descent; cost is O(depth), independent of training set size."
• Follow-up to expect: "Why is prediction so cheap compared to training?" — because training must search the (feature, threshold) space at every node (Topic 10), while prediction just walks a pre-built structure.
• Reflex to display: when asked "why did the tree predict X?", point to the path — and immediately note the leaf composition. The path is the audit trail; the leaf is the confidence.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Prediction = a deterministic walk from root to leaf, where each node asks one feature-threshold question.
  • A tree partitions feature space; every input that lands in the same leaf gets the same prediction. The tree doesn't retrieve similar examples — it labels regions.
  • The traversal path only sees the features along it — different predictions see different subsets of the tree's structure. This is the locality of feature importance.
  • Prediction cost is O(depth), independent of training set size — extraordinarily cheap to deploy at scale.
  • The path explains routing; the leaf composition explains confidence. Both must be audited; reading only the path is reading the audit trail without the audit.
  • Two parcels with very different unseen features can land in the same leaf — a leaf is a region, not a memory.
Journey rail ① Visualize→ ② Predict→ ③ Rules→ ④ Probability→ ⑤ CART→ ⑥ Diagnose

03 Topic 3 of 14

Decision Rules — The Tree as Plain-Language Logic

A path through the tree is a chain of predicates. Read those predicates back to back and you have an if/then rule — the same kind of rule a domain expert would write by hand, except the tree chose the predicates for you. This topic is where decision trees earn their "interpretable" reputation, and also where you'll see why that reputation is conditional.

🎬 The Story — Printing the tree on a laminated card

June demands the tree in plain English

Wednesday morning, June drops a stack of index cards on Ravi's desk. "Twenty cards. Each card has a parcel's three features. I want you to read me, out loud, the rule each parcel satisfies — not 'the tree predicts X,' but the actual if/then statement. I'm going to give this card stack to the dock team and they will read each other the rules. If they can't do it in 90 seconds, the system doesn't deploy."

Ravi reads the first card aloud: "If distance ≤ 17 km AND weight ≤ 320 g THEN priority." The second: "If distance ≤ 17 km AND weight > 320 g THEN standard." The third: "If distance > 17 km AND distance ≤ 50 km THEN standard." The fourth: "If distance > 50 km THEN economy." Four rules total. He pauses. "That's the entire model, in plain English."

Tomás looks up from his coffee. "That's the operational superpower of decision trees. A neural network with the same accuracy would be 14 million floating-point numbers; you can't read it to a dock team. A linear model is a weighted sum — readable in a different way, but the rule isn't a sentence, it's a multiplication. The tree is the only common model whose predictions arrive as language. That's why banks, hospitals, and insurers still use decision trees when their regulators demand 'explainability' — a regulation that asks 'why did you deny this loan?' is answered in seconds by a path; answered in months by a neural network."

💡 But here's the catch — the rules are only as good as the splits that produced them. A tree that split on a noisy feature (like a parcel's stock price, which the dock team doesn't even have) produces rules that read like English but don't operate like English. Topic 11's regularization is what keeps the rules sensible. For now, you just need to know how to read them.

⚡ Law 1 — Predict Before Explanation

Before You Learn: What Do You Think?

"If you had to describe the rule the Topic 1 tree uses to route a parcel as economy, what is the fewest conditions you need? Write the if/then statement before reading the answer."

The Correction

The fewest conditions: IF distance > 50 km THEN economy. That's it — a single predicate. On the Topic 1 tree, the path to the economy leaf is just distance ≤ 17 km? No → distance ≤ 50 km? No → economy leaf, which simplifies to distance > 50 km. Some leaves need multiple conditions; some need only one. The "shortest rule" depends on how the tree's structure groups predicates on the path.

The deeper insight: every root-to-leaf path is a conjunction of predicates — an AND-chain. distance ≤ 17 AND weight ≤ 320 is the priority rule. distance ≤ 17 AND weight > 320 is the standard-left rule. distance > 17 AND distance ≤ 50 is the standard-right rule. distance > 50 is the economy rule. Four conjunctions cover the whole feature space — that's the tree's complete decision logic, written as English.

What should surprise you?

Two things. First, the rule's length depends on the leaf's depth, not on the leaf's importance. The economy rule is one condition because the path is one split long; the priority rule is two conditions because the path is two splits long. Second, rules overlap in their antecedents — both priority and standard-left start with distance ≤ 17. That's not a bug; it's the tree sharing structure across leaves. A naive reader might miss the shared prefix and over-read the rules' complexity.

What changed in your mental model?

🧠 The idea, explained three ways

🧢 Everyday analogy

Imagine a decision your friend makes about whether to bike or bus to work: "If it's raining, I take the bus. If it's not raining but it's below 5°C, I take the bus. If it's not raining and above 5°C but I have a meeting before 9, I take the bus. Otherwise, I bike." That's four if/then rules — and they share a structure: the first three all end in "I take the bus." A decision tree produces exactly this kind of if/then collection, where the rules share antecedents.

🎬 In our story

The dock team's laminated card has four boxes — one per leaf — and each box is an if/then rule. The team reads the parcel's features, walks down the rules in order, and stops at the first one that matches. Two of the rules say priority/standard; one says standard; one says economy. The card fits in a shirt pocket. Ravi's job, when the tree updates: re-print the card and ship it to the dock. The whole ML deployment is, operationally, a paper update.

🔬 Technical view

Every root-to-leaf path is a conjunction of predicates — an AND-chain of feature-threshold tests. For a tree with L leaves, the tree partitions the feature space into L axis-aligned rectangles, each describable by exactly one conjunction. Formally, the rule for leaf ℓ is ∧ⱼ (x_j ≤ t_j OR x_j > t_j) over the features on the path — but in practice we just read the predicates in path order. The rule is the partition. There's no separate "explanation layer"; the partition is self-explaining.

From tree paths to plain-language rules

What should you notice? The rule length equals the leaf depth. The economy rule is one condition because its leaf is one level deep from the root's right child; the priority rule is two conditions because its leaf is two levels deep. A naive reader might confuse "short rule" with "simple concept" — but the economy rule is short only because the tree's structure sent it through a single split. The rule's quality comes from the leaf's composition, not from the rule's length.

The "if/then" reconstruction in scikit-learn

Scikit-learn's tree.export_text(clf) produces a text rendering of the tree as nested if/then rules — exactly the laminated-card format. The same library's tree.decision_path(X) produces a sparse indicator matrix showing which nodes were traversed for each input — useful for audit logs. For a more graphical export, plot_tree(clf) draws the tree with split predicates and leaf statistics. All three expose the same structure in different formats — but they all read out the same predicates and the same compositions. The tree doesn't have separate "model" and "explanation" representations; the structure is both.

🛠️ What "decision rules" mean to an engineer

The decision-rule view is the bridge between ML and operations. An operations team doesn't read probabilities or coefficients — they read rules. A trained tree produces, for free, a rule set that operations can laminate, distribute, and audit. This is why decision trees remain the dominant model in regulated industries (banking, insurance, healthcare) where regulations require "explainability" — the path is the explanation; there's no separate explainability layer to maintain.

🛠️ Reading the rules like a practitioner

Three checks on every rule set: (1) Coverage — do the rules partition the entire feature space with no gaps? (Yes, always, by construction.) (2) Overlap — do the rules overlap? (No, never, because each input lands in exactly one leaf.) (3) Sensibility — does each rule's antecedent make domain sense? (Often, but not always — a tree might split on a feature like stock price that operations can't measure in real time.) The third check is the human's job and the tree cannot do it.

🔴 Law 2 — Failure Modes Over Features

How This Breaks: when rules read like English but lie like a black box

🧬 Why was this needed?

Because stakeholders ask "why" — and most models can't answer in plain language. Decision rules are the bridge: the same model that does the math also produces the explanation, in the same artifact.

🤫 What it quietly assumes

That the rule's antecedent features are available at decision time. A tree that splits on a feature the dock team can't measure (say, the parcel's stock-price-correlated "risk score") produces a rule that reads like English but operates like a black box — the dock team can't execute it.

💀 How it fails silently

A rule with five antecedents is still readable English, but it's also a sign that the leaf is deep — and a deep leaf is a memorization candidate. The rule's length is a free signal of overfitting risk; nobody looks at it.

🔧 What happens next?

Topic 11's max_depth limits rule length. Topic 4 turns the rule's leaf composition into a probability estimate, so the rule can be flagged as "confident" or "borderline." Together, they make the rule both readable and honest.

Failure file — the rule that asked about a feature the dock didn't have

A tree-based loan approval system produced a rule: IF credit_score > 720 AND risk_adjusted_income_ratio < 0.18 AND prior_loan_defaults = 0 THEN approve. The first two features were computed in batch nightly; the third was a real-time query. The rule read like English — but the dock-equivalent loan officer couldn't execute it without waiting for batch. Approvals averaged 4 hours delay; the customer conversion rate dropped 18%. Lesson: a rule is only operational if every antecedent feature is available at decision time. The tree can't check this — only the deployment engineer can.

🧩 Important Terminology

Decision rule

Simple: an if/then statement the tree produces for free — the plain-language form of a root-to-leaf path.

Technical: a conjunction of feature-threshold predicates mapping to a leaf prediction; each leaf yields exactly one rule.

see glossary →

Threshold-based decision

Simple: a yes/no question about a feature: "is this feature at or below this number?"

Technical: a binary predicate x_j ≤ t; the basic building block of every internal node.

see glossary →

Recursive decision path

Simple: the chain of decisions from the root down to a leaf — a single prediction's audit trail.

Technical: the ordered conjunction of predicates traversed for a given input; equivalently, the unique root-to-leaf path whose every predicate the input satisfies.

see glossary →

Interpretability

Simple: the property that a human can read the model's reasoning and understand why a prediction was made.

Technical: a model's ability to expose a human-understandable explanation of its prediction; for trees, the path itself is the explanation — no separate explanation layer needed.

see glossary →

🟢 Law 3 — Compression Beats Coverage

Compress It

"Explain decision rules in one paragraph, as if you were explaining it to a 12-year-old."

Expert compression

Imagine a list of sentences, each starting with "if" and ending with a label. "If it's raining and you have an umbrella, walk. If it's raining and you don't, take the bus. If it's not raining and it's warm, bike." Each sentence is one rule. The list covers every possible weather state — there are no gaps and no overlaps. A decision tree produces exactly such a list, for free, by reading its root-to-leaf paths aloud. The sentences share prefixes ("if it's raining and…") because the tree shares structure. The list fits on a card; the card is the model.

One-diagram version
🍃 leaf→📝 read path predicates→🔗 AND-chain→📋 rule
One-sentence version

A decision rule is a leaf's root-to-leaf path read as an if/then statement — the tree produces one rule per leaf, for free.

Memory hook

📋 "Each leaf is a sentence."

🟡 Law 4 — Emotion Creates Judgment

Engineer Stakes

Scenario — the rule that referenced a feature ops couldn't measure

A triage system produced a rule: IF distance ≤ 17 AND weight ≤ 320 AND declared_value > 200 THEN priority. The first two features were measured at the dock in seconds; the third was the customer-declared value, which arrived via a CSV from procurement 90 minutes after the parcel hit the dock. The dock team routed 14 parcels by the rule's first two conditions only — and missed the priority routing on three $250+ parcels. The customer demanded $1,200 in surcharges. June's question: did anyone audit the rule's operational feasibility?

What went wrong? The rule read like English but executed like a black box — the dock team couldn't measure all three antecedents in real time. Was the rule wrong or the deployment? The deployment — the rule was mathematically correct; the deployment ignored feature availability. What evidence should have been collected? A per-rule "feature availability audit" listing which antecedent features are real-time vs. batch. What should be changed first? Either retrain excluding declared_value (if it adds little), or change the rule to "two-of-three antecedents → escalate to a human sorter." What should NOT be changed blindly? Don't rip out the value feature if it adds information — restructure the deployment instead.

🏗️ Build in Public Challenge

Take the tree you built in Topic 1 and write out every leaf's rule as a single if/then sentence. Then audit each rule: are all antecedent features available at decision time? Is any rule's leaf composition borderline (5-of-9 or worse)? Is any rule longer than three antecedents (a depth-of-3 leaf, a possible memorization)? Post the audit — three checks per rule, in plain English.

🟣 Law 5 — AI Accelerates, Humans Judge

AI vs Human Judgment — Decision rules

🤖 AI Should Handle

  • Rendering the trained tree as text rules via export_text or as a graph via plot_tree
  • Enumerating every root-to-leaf path as a separate if/then sentence
  • Detecting rules with long antecedent chains (depth ≥ 5) for overfitting review
  • Drafting a "rule coverage report" showing how many training examples each rule covers
  • Suggesting simpler alternative rules (e.g., pruning candidates)

🧑‍⚖️ Humans Must Own

  • Are all antecedent features measurable at decision time? (Operational audit.)
  • Do the rule antecedents match domain intuition — does "distance ≤ 17" mean "priority-truck catchment"?
  • Is the rule length (depth) excessive for the example count? (A 6-antecedent rule on 9 examples is memorization.)
  • Do the rules overlap in problematic ways, or are they cleanly disjoint? (Disjoint by construction, but humans must verify the partition is sensible.)
  • The call: ship the rule card, escalate, or re-train?
What would you ask AI?"Here is my trained decision tree. Export every root-to-leaf path as an if/then rule in plain English. For each rule, list (1) the antecedent features in path order, (2) whether each feature is measurable in real-time at the dock, (3) the leaf's class composition, and (4) the rule's depth. Flag any rule with depth > 3 or composition majority < 0.7."
What must you verify yourself? Check operational feasibility — every antecedent feature must be measurable in real time at the dock, or the rule is unexecutable. Sanity-check rule sensibility — does "distance ≤ 17 km" match operational reality (the priority-truck catchment)? And look at rule depth — AI-generated rule reports reliably list depth but won't spontaneously flag "this depth-6 rule on 9 examples is a memorization." AI can render the rules; only you can certify the rules are operational and well-founded.

🎤 Interview Question

✅ Quick Check — Decision Rules
🧒 Beginner lens

A decision rule is just an if/then sentence the tree writes for free. Each leaf of the tree becomes one rule: "if these conditions are true, then this is the answer." The rules share prefixes (like "if distance ≤ 17 km AND...") because the tree's structure is shared across leaves. The whole model fits on a laminated card the dock team can read in 90 seconds — that's the operational superpower of decision trees.

🔬 Technical lens

Every root-to-leaf path is a conjunction of predicates — an AND-chain of x_j ≤ t tests. With L leaves, the tree partitions feature space into L axis-aligned rectangles, each describable by exactly one conjunction. Scikit-learn exposes the rules via tree.export_text(clf) (text) and plot_tree(clf) (graphical). The rule's length equals the leaf's depth — a free signal of overfitting risk. The rules are disjoint by construction (each input lands in exactly one leaf) and complete by construction (every input lands in some leaf) — these are mathematical guarantees, not engineering choices.

🎤 Interview lens

• "A decision rule is a leaf's root-to-leaf path read as an if/then statement; the tree produces one rule per leaf, for free."
• Follow-up to expect: "Why is the rule's length a signal of overfitting?" — because rule length equals leaf depth, and a deep leaf is a memorization candidate.
• Reflex to display: distinguish "rule is readable" from "rule is operational" — a rule with antecedent features the dock can't measure reads like English but executes like a black box.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Every root-to-leaf path is a conjunction of feature-threshold predicates — an if/then rule the tree produces for free.
  • A tree with L leaves produces exactly L rules; the rules are disjoint and complete by construction (each input lands in exactly one leaf).
  • The rule's length equals the leaf's depth — a free signal of overfitting risk nobody looks at.
  • Rules share antecedent prefixes across leaves (like a trie) — the tree shares structure, but a naive reader might miss this and overestimate complexity.
  • A rule is only operational if every antecedent feature is measurable at decision time — the tree cannot verify this; only the deployment engineer can.
  • Decision trees are the dominant model in regulated industries because the path is the explanation; no separate explainability layer is needed.

04 Topic 4 of 14

Estimating Class Probabilities — The Leaf as a Confidence Report

Topic 2 ended with a leaf label, Topic 3 with a rule. Both left a question on the table: how confident is the model? The answer is sitting inside the leaf already — not as a separate score, but as the leaf's class composition. The 8-of-9 priority leaf is not just a "priority" prediction; it is a probability distribution, and reading it changes how the tree is deployed.

🎬 The Story — A confidence number for the laminated card

June asks: "how confident is the leaf?"

Friday morning, June walks the dock team through the laminated card from Topic 3. The sorters read the rules, run a few sample parcels, and nod — until one of them, a dock veteran named Marisol, raises her hand. "The card says priority. But it also says 8-of-9 priority. What's the 1-of-9? Is that a mistake, or is the model 11% wrong?" June turns to Ravi. "Good question. How confident is the prediction?"

Ravi opens the trained tree's predict_proba method on his laptop and runs the 4:14 a.m. parcel through it. The model returns [0.889, 0.111, 0.0] — a three-number vector, one probability per class. "The leaf is more than a label," he says, slowly. "It's a composition. Eight of nine training parcels in this leaf were priority; one was standard. The model treats those proportions as the probability estimate. The leaf doesn't just say priority — it says 89% priority, 11% standard, 0% economy. The label is the argmax; the vector is the confidence."

Tomás leans in. "And that vector is what your deployment contract should read. A leaf with 0.55 priority and 0.45 standard is a coin flip wearing a label — you don't ship it the same way you ship a 0.99 leaf. June, you want the laminated card to show the percentage next to the label. The dock team doesn't need a second model; they need to read what the leaf already knows." June nods, taking a red pen to the card: each leaf now reads "priority — 89%" instead of just "priority."

💡 A leaf is more than a label — it is the model's best estimate of how the answer's probability is distributed. The majority class is the prediction; the proportion vector is the confidence. And there's a trap: a 1-of-1 leaf produces 100% probability, which is the most confident and the least trustworthy kind of confidence — memorization dressed as certainty. Topic 11 fixes the leaf sizes; for now, learn to read the vector.

🍃 leaf→ 📊 class-count vector→ ➗ normalize by N→ 📈 probability vector→ 🏷️ argmax → label · vector → confidence Leaf → counts → normalize → probability vector. The leaf is its own confidence report.

⚡ Law 1 — Predict Before Explanation

Before You Learn: What Do You Think?

"A leaf contains 8 priority / 1 standard / 0 economy training examples. What is the model's class-probability estimate for priority? And is that probability well-calibrated?"

The Correction

The estimate for priority is 8 / 9 ≈ 0.889 (88.9%), and the full vector is [0.889, 0.111, 0.000]. The model computes this by simply dividing each class count by the leaf's total sample count — what statisticians call the maximum-likelihood estimate of the class probability under i.i.d. multinomial sampling. There is no smoothing, no shrinkage, no calibration layer by default. The leaf is its own probability report.

Is that probability well-calibrated? Not necessarily. Calibration asks a different question: if the model says "89% priority" on a hundred different leaves, do roughly 89 of those predictions turn out to be priority in production? An untrained decision tree has no reason to satisfy that property — its proportions reflect training frequency, not deployment probability. If the training data is representative, the estimate is approximately calibrated; if the training data is biased or stale, the estimate inherits that bias. A 1-of-1 leaf produces a 100% probability estimate that is the worst kind of confidence: memorization dressed as certainty.

What should surprise you?

Two things. First, that the probability estimate is computed for free from data the tree already has — there is no separate probability model bolted on; the leaf's training composition is the probability estimate. Second, that a tiny leaf can produce an extreme (100%) probability, while a huge leaf with the same majority share (e.g., 800-of-900 priority) produces the same 89% estimate. The estimate doesn't know its own sample size — you have to read the count separately.

What changed in your mental model?

🧠 The idea, explained three ways

🧢 Everyday analogy

Imagine a 9-sided die where 8 faces are green and 1 face is yellow. If I ask "what's the probability the next roll is green?" you'd say 8/9 — about 89%. You don't need to know anything about how the die was made; you just count the faces. A decision-tree leaf is exactly such a die: its training members are the faces, the class counts are the colors, and the probability estimate is just the face count divided by 9. The catch — you've only rolled this die a handful of times, so the true proportions might be different from your 8/9 estimate.

🎬 In our story

June's laminated card now shows, next to each leaf's label, a percentage in red ink. The priority leaf reads "priority — 89%." The standard-right leaf reads "standard — 53%." The economy leaf reads "economy — 100%." The dock team knows: anything below 70% gets routed to a human sorter as a fallback. The card hasn't gotten more complicated; it's gotten more honest. A label hides uncertainty; a percentage exposes it.

🔬 Technical view

A leaf stores its training-subset class-count vector (n₁, n₂, …, n_K) where K is the number of classes. The class-probability estimate is p̂_k = n_k / N where N = Σn_k — the maximum-likelihood estimator under the i.i.d. multinomial model. The predicted label is argmax_k p̂_k. Scikit-learn exposes this via tree.predict_proba(X). The estimator is uncalibrated by default — the proportions reflect training frequency, not deployment probability. Calibration can be added later via Platt scaling or isotonic regression, but only with held-out data; the raw leaf is uncalibrated.

Why this matters in a real ML system

Because downstream logic consumes probabilities, not labels. Expected-value computations ("if I route this priority, what's the expected cost?"), fallback rules ("escalate if max probability < 0.7"), threshold tuning (Topic 17 in earlier chapters), and ensemble averaging (Chapter 7) all need a probability, not a hard label. A decision tree is one of the few models where the probability estimate is computed from the same data structure as the prediction — no separate head, no sigmoid layer, no softmax. That's a feature; it's also a liability, because the estimate inherits the leaf's sample-size problems directly.

A leaf is a probability vector, not just a label

What should you notice? The probability bar and the leaf's tile grid are the same object rendered two ways: one as colored counts, one as normalized proportions. There is no separate "probability model" — the leaf's training composition is the probability estimate. And note the asymmetry: a 1-of-1 leaf would render as a single green tile and a 100% bar — the most confident and the least trustworthy kind of probability.

The lab shows the leaf's tile grid, the probability vector, the argmax prediction, and the Gini impurity — all updating live. Try a 1-of-1 leaf to see how a 100% probability emerges from a single training example. Then try a 5/4 leaf to see how a coin-flip composition hides behind a confident label.
